montirelin.summary: A lab-stable TRH analogue people discuss for alertness and energy that keeps training and routines consistent; studied in animals for arousal.

quick.overview:
Montirelin is a modified version of the hormone TRH, built to last longer and act more strongly in the brain. People who discuss it in peptide and nootropic circles are after more wakefulness, energy and focus, which they link to staying consistent with training and daily routines.

The chain is indirect: stronger central arousal, then better energy and focus, then steadier training. It has been tested in rodents and cell cultures for memory, arousal and neuroprotection, and the human record is a brief reported study in patients with impaired consciousness. In animal brains it binds TRH receptors, raises TSH and prolactin, and stimulates cholinergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic activity.
quick.how: It circulates as a research peptide in nootropic and recovery discussions rather than as a product with a standard routine. Users who mention it describe pairing it with sleep, training and focus-oriented stacks, and there is no established timeline for results.
quick.risks: No safety profile in healthy people has been published in the sources reviewed. Animal studies report effects on blood pressure and heart rate, and its endocrine actions mirror TRH. It is not described as an approved drug and is sold for laboratory use.

angle.text: Montirelin is a stable TRH analogue that people discuss for wakefulness and energy, with the idea that more alertness means steadier training and routines. That link to looks runs through consistency rather than any direct effect. Research so far is in animals, studying arousal and neuroprotection.

glypromate.summary: GPE, a small IGF-1-derived peptide studied for brain protection and recovery; its analogue trofinetide became an approved Rett syndrome drug.

quick.overview:
Glypromate (GPE) is a three-amino-acid piece of IGF-1. People discuss it for brain protection and recovery, with the hope that better recovery and focus translate into steadier training and routines.

In lab research it has been examined as a neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory signal derived from IGF-1. Because the plain peptide breaks down quickly and crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, more stable analogues were developed, and the best known, trofinetide, was approved in 2023 for Rett syndrome. No human trial of glypromate itself is described in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It appears in peptide catalogues and discussions as a brain and recovery compound, often alongside other nootropic peptides. There is no standard routine or timeline for appearance-related results.
quick.risks: It is experimental and not approved. No human safety data for the unmodified peptide were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Glypromate (GPE) is an IGF-1-derived tripeptide that people discuss for brain protection and recovery, tying better focus and recovery to steadier training. Research is laboratory neuroprotection work, and its analogue trofinetide is an approved Rett syndrome drug.

trofinetide.summary: An oral prescription drug for Rett syndrome and an analogue of GPE; it is a disease treatment, with no appearance use documented.

quick.overview:
Trofinetide is an oral prescription drug for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder. It is a stabilised copy of a small IGF-1 fragment and was approved by the US FDA in March 2023, the first drug approved for the condition.

It shows up in peptide discussions because of its relation to GPE (glypromate). It is thought to dampen neuroinflammation and support neuronal signalling through IGF-1-related pathways. Approval rests on a 12-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in patients aged two and older; no appearance use is documented.
quick.how: It is given by prescription as an oral treatment for Rett syndrome, under clinician supervision. It is used in that medical setting rather than as a looks product.
quick.risks: Diarrhea and vomiting are the most common adverse effects in trials. It is prescription-only, with limited data in kidney impairment.

angle.text: Trofinetide is an approved prescription drug for Rett syndrome and a GPE analogue, so it comes up in peptide discussions as a relative of glypromate. It is used and studied as a disease treatment, and no appearance use is documented.

fosgonimeton.summary: An investigational Alzheimer's drug that acts as a prodrug of dihexa, developed for cognition rather than appearance.

quick.overview:
Fosgonimeton is an investigational drug from Athira Pharma that was tested for Alzheimer's disease and other dementias. It is a prodrug of dihexa, a compound popular in nootropic circles, and it boosts HGF/MET signalling.

It was developed to support brain health and cognition, not for any cosmetic purpose. Preclinical studies report effects on neuronal health, and published human data consist of a phase I trial in healthy volunteers and people with Alzheimer's plus a registered phase 2/3 trial. No appearance data exist.
quick.how: It was given in clinical trials, not sold as a product. In looksmaxxing and longevity-oriented communities it mostly appears as a related name to dihexa.
quick.risks: It is not approved for any use anywhere. A phase I trial reported on safety and tolerability; details of later-phase results are in the primary literature.

angle.text: Fosgonimeton is an investigational Alzheimer's drug that works as a prodrug of dihexa, a name known in nootropic circles for cognition. It was developed for dementia, not appearance, and the research on it is clinical work on cognition.

bnn-20.summary: A DHEA-derived BDNF-mimicking compound studied in Parkinson's mouse models for brain protection.

quick.overview:
BNN-20 is a lab-made steroid-like compound, described by its developers as a "microneurotrophin", meant to mimic the brain growth factor BDNF. People in research-chemical circles discuss it for brain protection and cognitive support.

It is derived from DHEA, crosses the blood-brain barrier and is reported to lack endocrine side effects. It acts through the TrkB receptor and reduces neuroinflammation in mouse models, mainly the "weaver" mouse model of Parkinson's-like dopamine neuron loss. No human studies exist and no appearance use is documented.
quick.how: It is discussed in longevity and nootropic circles as a neurotrophin mimic. There is no established human routine or timeline.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown because no clinical trials are published. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: BNN-20 is a DHEA-derived BDNF mimic discussed in research-chemical circles for brain protection and cognitive support. No appearance use is documented; the research is preclinical, mainly Parkinson's mouse models.

bnn-27.summary: A DHEA-derived NGF-mimicking compound studied in cells and mice for nerve and brain protection.

quick.overview:
BNN-27 is a lab-made steroid-like molecule meant to imitate nerve growth factor (NGF). People in research-chemical circles discuss it for nerve and brain protection.

It is a DHEA analogue reported to bind the NGF receptors TrkA and p75NTR with high affinity, cross the blood-brain barrier and lack DHEA's hormonal activity. In mouse models it showed neuroprotective and neurogenic effects. Research is preclinical, with no human trials and no appearance use documented.
quick.how: It is discussed in nootropic and longevity circles as an NGF mimetic. No established human routine or timeline exists.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: BNN-27 is a DHEA-derived NGF mimetic that its developers describe as lacking hormonal activity, and it is discussed for nerve and brain protection. No appearance use is documented; the research is preclinical.

n-acetyl-selank-amidate.summary: An acetylated, amidated Selank analogue sold as a research chemical for calmer mood and social ease.

quick.overview:
N-Acetyl Selank Amidate is a chemically modified version of the peptide Selank, with changes meant to help it resist breakdown and last longer in the body. Users hope for a calmer mood and more social ease than the parent peptide gives.

The chain is indirect: less anxiety and stress, a calmer and more composed demeanour, and better social presence. It is presumed to act like Selank, which is described as modulating GABAergic signalling. No studies of this exact compound are reported, and the benefits are extrapolated from Selank research.
quick.how: It is sold by research-chemical suppliers for laboratory use. Users describe it as a longer-lasting alternative to Selank, with no established routine or timeline.
quick.risks: It is not approved for human use in most jurisdictions. Safety in people has not been studied.

angle.text: This acetylated, amidated Selank analogue is sold as a research chemical, with users hoping for less anxiety, a calmer demeanour and more social ease. The link to looks runs through composure and presence. The analogue itself has no direct studies; the research relates to Selank.

n-acetyl-semax-amidate.summary: An acetylated, amidated Semax analogue sold as a research chemical for sharper focus and stamina.

quick.overview:
N-Acetyl Semax Amidate is a chemically modified version of the peptide Semax, with changes meant to help it resist breakdown and last longer in the body. Users seek sharper focus and stamina than the parent peptide gives.

The chain is indirect: better focus and cognition, more productivity and consistency, steadier training and routine. It is presumed to act like Semax, which is described as affecting neurotrophin (BDNF, NGF) expression in animal studies. No studies of this exact compound are reported; the benefits are extrapolated from Semax research.
quick.how: It is sold by research-chemical suppliers for laboratory use. Intranasal use is the route typically described for Semax-type peptides, and no established timeline exists.
quick.risks: It is not approved for human use in most jurisdictions. Safety in people has not been studied.

angle.text: This acetylated, amidated Semax analogue is sold as a research chemical, with users seeking sharper focus and stamina that carry into steadier training and routines. Any link to looks runs through habit consistency. The analogue itself has no direct studies; the research relates to Semax.

dnsp-11.summary: An experimental GDNF-derived brain peptide studied in rats and monkeys for dopamine neuron support.

quick.overview:
DNSP-11 is an 11-amino-acid peptide derived from the precursor region of GDNF, a protein that supports dopamine neurons. People in nootropic circles discuss it for dopamine neuron support and possible brain and mood benefits.

It was proposed as a smaller, easier-to-deliver alternative to full-length GDNF for Parkinson's disease research. In rat experiments it changed dopamine neuron function and increased ERK 1/2 signalling in cells. Published studies are in cells, rats and rhesus macaques, delivered directly to the brain or repeatedly through the nose. No human trials were found and no appearance data exist.
quick.how: It appears in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues. No established human routine or timeline exists.
quick.risks: Its safety in humans has not been studied in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal findings do not establish human effects.

angle.text: DNSP-11 is an experimental GDNF-derived peptide discussed in nootropic circles for dopamine neuron support, brain and mood. No appearance use is documented; it has been studied in rats and monkeys with no human trials.

fgl.summary: A lab-made fragment of a neural adhesion protein studied in rodents for memory and brain plasticity.

quick.overview:
FGL is a 15-amino-acid peptide taken from NCAM, a protein involved in nerve-cell adhesion and plasticity. People in nootropic circles discuss it for memory and brain plasticity.

It is reported to act as an FGFR1 agonist, promoting neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in cultured rat neurons and changing synaptic structure in aged rats. Studies cover memory, social recognition, ageing and Alzheimer's-type models in rodents. No human trials or appearance data were found.
quick.how: It appears in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues. No established human routine or timeline exists.
quick.risks: Human safety has not been established in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal findings do not establish human effects.

angle.text: FGL is a synthetic fragment of a neural adhesion protein discussed in nootropic circles for memory and brain plasticity. No appearance use is documented; the research is rodent memory data with no human trials.

cenegermin.summary: A prescription nerve growth factor eye drop approved for a rare corneal disease; it is a medical treatment with no appearance use.

quick.overview:
Cenegermin (Oxervate) is a recombinant human nerve growth factor eye drop, approved in the EU in 2017 and the US in 2018 for neurotrophic keratitis, a rare condition in which damaged corneal nerves lead to persistent surface defects. It is the first drug approved for that condition.

It acts on the TrkA and p75NTR receptors and was developed to address the nerve-related cause of corneal breakdown. In registration trials, most adults with moderate or severe disease reached complete corneal healing within about eight weeks. It comes up in peptide discussions as an NGF product, and no cosmetic studies were found.
quick.how: It is prescribed by eye clinicians as a drop for a defined course in neurotrophic keratitis. It is used as a medical treatment, not as a cosmetic.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects include eye pain, inflammation, increased tearing, eyelid pain and a foreign-body sensation. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Cenegermin is a prescription nerve growth factor eye drop that heals the corneal surface in neurotrophic keratitis, and it comes up in peptide discussions as an NGF product. It is studied and approved for that rare corneal disease; no appearance use is documented.

mecasermin-rinfabate.summary: An IGF-1/IGFBP-3 injectable built for rare growth failure in children; no data covers height in people with normal growth.

quick.overview:
Mecasermin rinfabate (Iplex) pairs recombinant IGF-1 with its binding protein and is injected under the skin. Insmed developed it for children with severe IGF-1 deficiency or growth hormone insensitivity, and height-focused forum posters sometimes ask whether IGF-1 products could add height.

Binding IGF-1 to IGFBP-3 was designed to extend how long IGF-1 stays in circulation and to reduce side effects such as low blood sugar. It was withdrawn for short-stature indications after a patent settlement, and trials moved to myotonic dystrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and retinopathy of prematurity. No studies address height in people with normal growth.
quick.how: It was given by daily injection under medical supervision in patient populations. It is a prescription biologic and is not used as a routine height product.
quick.risks: Reported effects in trials included lab changes such as higher testosterone and LDL in myotonic dystrophy patients. It is a prescription biologic, and published safety data come from patient populations.

angle.text: Mecasermin rinfabate is an IGF-1/IGFBP-3 injectable made for rare growth failure, and height-focused posters ask whether IGF-1 products could add height through more bone growth. It was studied in children with growth disorders; no data covers height in people with normal growth.

axokine.summary: A discontinued CNTF-based injectable developed for obesity that produced modest weight loss in trials.

quick.overview:
Axokine is a modified version of CNTF, a nerve survival protein, that Regeneron developed as an obesity drug after weight loss was noticed when CNTF was given for motor neuron disease. It was meant to lower body weight through a leptin-like appetite signal.

In phase III trials around 2003, patients without antibodies lost about 12.5 pounds over a year versus 4.5 pounds on placebo, and nearly 70 percent developed antibodies after about three months. In diabetic mice it was reported to raise metabolic rate beyond its effect on food intake. It was not commercialised and is mentioned as a historical fat-loss compound.
quick.how: It was given by injection in clinical trials. It was never marketed, so there is no everyday routine.
quick.risks: Antibody formation against the drug was the major issue reported in trials. It is not an approved or marketed drug.

angle.text: Axokine is a CNTF-based injectable developed as an obesity drug that lowers body weight through a leptin-like mechanism: less appetite, lower intake, lower weight. It was discontinued after trials showed modest weight loss and antibodies in most users, and it is mentioned as a historical fat-loss compound.

kttks.summary: The collagen-signalling pentapeptide behind Matrixyl, used in anti-wrinkle skincare to smooth fine lines.

quick.overview:
KTTKS is a five-amino-acid peptide, usually attached to a palmitoyl fat chain (Pal-KTTKS) and sold as Matrixyl in anti-wrinkle products since 2000. People use it to smooth fine lines and firm skin.

It is a matrikine, a messenger peptide reported to stimulate extracellular matrix and collagen synthesis in skin cells, and the fat chain is meant to aid penetration. A 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55 assessed it in photoaged facial skin and reported improvement, and lab work shows it raises collagen production in cultured fibroblasts. Reviewers discuss how well the peptide reaches the dermis.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on serum or cream ingredient, typically as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Studies of it ran for around 12 weeks.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed do not report safety problems. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

angle.text: KTTKS, sold as Matrixyl in palmitoylated form, is a collagen-signalling peptide used in anti-wrinkle skincare. It signals skin cells to make more collagen and matrix, which smooths fine lines. A 93-subject split-face trial studied it, and skin penetration is discussed in the literature.

palmitoyl-tripeptide-38.summary: A branded cosmetic signal peptide added to serums and creams to boost collagen and firm skin.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 (Matrixyl Synthe'6, from Sederma) is a lab-made peptide added to anti-wrinkle serums and creams. The supplier says it prompts skin to make more collagen types I, III and IV, fibronectin, hyaluronic acid and laminin-5, for firmer, smoother skin.

It is described as a matrikine mimic: a small signalling fragment meant to trigger the skin's matrix-building cells, with a palmitoyl fatty chain to help it mix with skin lipids. Most efficacy figures come from supplier testing, including a small double-blind study of 25 women using a 2% cream. Independent studies test finished products with many ingredients, so the peptide's own contribution is not separated out.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in daily leave-on serums and moisturizers, usually alongside other actives.
quick.risks: A 55-person patch test of one serum containing it reported no irritation. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and long-term data specific to the peptide are limited.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a cosmetic signal peptide sold as a collagen booster: it signals skin to remodel its matrix for firmer, smoother skin. The most detailed results come from supplier data and multi-ingredient serum studies.

glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline.summary: A collagen-derived tripeptide found in oral collagen supplements, which people take for skin firmness and hydration.

quick.overview:
Gly-Pro-Hyp is one of the small peptides produced when collagen is broken down into the hydrolysates sold as oral collagen supplements and used in some cosmetics. People take those supplements for firmer, more hydrated, less wrinkled skin.

The idea is that collagen peptides are absorbed after eating and signal to skin fibroblasts. In rats, hydrolysates are reported to enter the blood partly as intact peptides. Research on this tripeptide covers how it is measured in products and how it is absorbed in laboratory and animal work; human skin trials have used collagen hydrolysates rather than the isolated peptide.
quick.how: It is taken as part of collagen hydrolysate powders, drinks or capsules as a daily supplement, and it is also found in some cosmetic products.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to the isolated tripeptide were found. It is not a regulated drug.

angle.text: Gly-Pro-Hyp is a collagen-derived tripeptide found in oral collagen supplements, taken for skin firmness and wrinkles. It is absorbed in animals and is thought to signal skin fibroblasts. Human skin trials have used collagen hydrolysates rather than the peptide itself.

ahk-cu.summary: A copper tripeptide marketed in hair-care products for thicker, fuller hair, studied so far in cultured follicle cells.

quick.overview:
AHK-Cu is a copper-bound three-amino-acid peptide (alanyl-histidyl-lysine, copper tripeptide-3) sold in hair-care products and related to the better-known GHK-Cu. People use it hoping for a longer hair growth phase, thicker hairs and a fuller scalp.

In a laboratory study on cultured human hair follicle cells, a tripeptide-copper complex was reported to boost fibroblast growth and VEGF and to act on dermal papilla cells, the cells that steer hair follicle growth. No human hair-growth trial of AHK-Cu was found.
quick.how: It is used as a topical ingredient in scalp serums and hair-care products, usually as part of a regular routine alongside other hair treatments.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy data specific to AHK-Cu were found.

angle.text: AHK-Cu is a copper tripeptide marketed in hair-care products and discussed as a hair-growth ingredient, much as GHK-Cu is for skin. It is thought to act on follicle cells for a longer growth phase and thicker hairs. Published work so far is a cell-culture study.

ll-37.summary: The body's own antimicrobial skin peptide, discussed for clearing acne and healing skin.

quick.overview:
LL-37 is a natural antimicrobial peptide made by skin and immune cells, and the only cathelicidin humans make. Forum posters discuss it for clearing acne, healing skin and anti-aging, drawing on its role in fighting skin bacteria and calming inflammation.

It damages microbial membranes and attracts immune cells through the FPRL1 receptor, and vitamin D raises its production. Published research is mainly on its natural role in skin infection and in atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea. The few registered LL-37 trials involve melanoma and diabetic foot ulcers; no trial for acne or cosmetic skin improvement was found.
quick.how: It is discussed in appearance communities as a research peptide for acne or skin quality. It is investigational, with no standard routine or established timeline.
quick.risks: It is investigational and not an approved drug. Excess LL-37 is suspected in rosacea and psoriasis inflammation. No safety data for cosmetic use were found.

angle.text: LL-37 is the body's own antimicrobial skin peptide, and forum posters discuss it for clearing acne, healing skin and anti-aging by lowering acne bacteria and inflammation. These uses draw on its immune biology; research covers skin infection and inflammatory skin disease.

heberprot-p.summary: A Cuban injectable EGF used for diabetic foot ulcers, and a reference point in discussions of EGF for skin healing.

quick.overview:
Heberprot-P is an injectable formulation of recombinant human epidermal growth factor (EGF), made by Cuba's Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology and marketed by Heber Biotec. It is used for advanced diabetic foot ulcers, and it comes up in discussions of EGF for skin healing and renewal.

EGF stimulates skin cell growth. In patients with ulcers it is injected into and around the wound base to promote granulation tissue and faster wound closure. Human reports are mostly small series plus one registered phase 3 trial, all in ulcers; no studies of cosmetic use were found.
quick.how: It is given by clinicians into and around the wound as a medical treatment. It is not used as a cosmetic product.
quick.risks: It is a medical product given by clinicians, and per Wikipedia it was not approved in the US as of 2016. Safety information in the sources reviewed is limited.

angle.text: Heberprot-P is a Cuban injectable EGF used for diabetic foot ulcers, where it stimulates cell growth for faster wound closure, and it comes up in discussions of EGF for skin healing. Wound-healing evidence is small-scale and covers ulcers.

palifermin.summary: A prescription keratinocyte growth factor that protects mouth and gut lining in cancer treatment, mentioned in skin-renewal discussions.

quick.overview:
Palifermin (Kepivance) is a truncated recombinant human keratinocyte growth factor (KGF) given intravenously. It is approved to reduce the incidence and duration of severe oral mucositis in patients with blood cancers receiving high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell support.

It binds the KGF receptor on epithelial cells, which is reported to boost their growth, maturation and migration. Because the US label notes the receptor is present in skin, hair follicles and sebaceous glands, it is occasionally mentioned in skin-renewal discussions. The evidence is for mucositis; no cosmetic studies were found.
quick.how: It is given by intravenous infusion in hospital cancer care. It is used as supportive treatment, not as a cosmetic.
quick.risks: The label lists rash, fever, raised amylase, itching and swelling as common, and flags uncertain effects on tumors expressing KGF receptors and possible fetal harm. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Palifermin is a prescription keratinocyte growth factor that stimulates epithelial cell growth, and it is occasionally mentioned in skin-renewal discussions. It is approved for chemotherapy mouth sores, which is where the evidence lies.
